SEEDANCE 2.0 vs GEMINI OMNI FLASH

Two giants. Two difficult 10-second scenes. Four attempts each. No excuses.

I used GPT Image 2 to create the storyboard for both scenes (attached), then sent both models into battle.

Gemini Omni Flash:

Worse visuals. Worse motion. Worse action. Overall, the result was still decent — but honestly, I expected more.

However: in all 4 attempts, Gemini actually followed the key instruction: the panda delivered the package to the boy.

Seedance 2.0:

This type of task is usually its battlefield — and visually, it shows.

Better transitions, stronger motion, more energy, more style. It simply looks cooler.

BUT: in every Seedance attempt, the panda didn’t deliver the package to the boy — it took the package from him instead.

So once again, this confirms what I’ve seen in previous tests:

Gemini Omni Flash = more accurate 
Seedance 2.0 = more cinematic

One follows instructions better. 
The other makes prettier mistakes.

What matters more to you: accuracy or spectacle?

posts.author: youralphamom
posts.text:
New AI video test: the legendary T-1000 finger wag from Terminator 2 — this time using image-to-video.

And somehow, Seedance 2.0 managed to disappoint me again.

Gemini Omni Flash, Seedance 2.0, Grok Imagine 1.5, and Kling 3.0 Pro were all given the same challenge: recreate that iconic side-to-side finger motion.

About six months ago, this was practically impossible. Back then I was mostly working with Veo 3.1, and the model simply couldn’t understand the gesture.

This time, every model technically completed it.

But some completed it… and some “completed” it.

As always, each model received exactly four attempts.

Here’s what happened:

- Gemini Omni Flash:

Another clear win.

For several motion and body-physics tests in a row, Omni has handled instructions that the other models struggle to understand.

The movement looked controlled, confident, and surprisingly realistic. It was easily the most convincing result of the entire comparison.

At this point, Omni is becoming the model to beat in precision-motion tests.

- Kling 3.0 Pro:

The weakest result by far.

The finger moved nicely in rhythm with the music. That’s about the only compliment I can give it.

The motion looked stiff, unsettling, and strangely doll-like. It technically moved the finger, but the result felt completely wrong.

This test made Kling look old. A new version is seriously overdue.

- Grok Imagine 1.5:

For the second test in a row, Grok somehow avoided embarrassing itself.

It clearly lost to Omni, but the result was still acceptable for such a specific and difficult movement.

The motion wasn’t perfect, but it understood the assignment well enough — and honestly, I liked the result.

- Seedance 2.0:

Another disappointment.

Seedance remains incredible at complex action scenes, but this is now the second test in a row where it struggled with a much smaller and more precise body movement.

Yes, the finger moves. But the result simply isn’t good enough, especially from a model as powerful as Seedance.

This seems to be one of its real weaknesses: huge action, great. Subtle controlled motion, surprisingly shaky.

Final ranking:

1. Gemini Omni Flash — another dominant win in motion and physics

2. Grok Imagine 1.5 — average, but without Omni, “average” would have been enough to win

3. Seedance 2.0 — another weak result in a precision-motion test

4. Kling 3.0 Pro — still usable, but clearly showing its age

Maybe the next test should be something inspired by GTA 6?

Seedance probably needs an action test to repair its reputation 😂

What should I test next?

posts.text:
I got early access to @openart_ai's Director tool, which lets you make multi-minute long videos with a unified agent. You can provide images, video, and even audio inputs to use, and the agent will plan it out. You can give feedback and it will produce a video for you.

I decided to test it with a really hard task where I provided lots of graphs and charts that were text and data heavy, which was pretty much the hardest thing I could have thrown at it. I wasn’t expecting perfection, but this shows the strengths and weaknesses.

Where it was really good:
1. I really liked the speech. It matched the voice reference I provided perfectly, and the audio quality was excellent.
2. Transitions were high quality. It seems to be using a good video model.

The issue was it didn't perfectly keep the text and data coherent. Words and numbers would be jumbled up, and sometimes there would be total gibberish. I don't think that's OpenArt’s problem; I think that is just the state of the art right now. Until we get better models available, this is the best we have got.

Perhaps Gemini Omni Pro will be able to reach the full coherence that is needed for this task. But the product itself was really good and followed feedback well; it is only limited by the state of the art models we have right now.

posts.author: youralphamom
posts.text:
New tongue-physics test for the best AI video models!

Seedance 2.0, Kling 3.0 Pro, Gemini Omni Flash, and Grok Imagine 1.5 were given a task that sounds ridiculously simple for a human:

Rotate the tongue in a continuous circle for 10 seconds. That’s it.

Each model received exactly four attempts.

Yet this tiny movement turned into an unexpectedly brutal test of instruction following, anatomy, motion consistency, and basic physical control.

And the result will probably surprise a lot of AI video creators. Spoiler: Seedance 2.0 completely failed to live up to its reputation this time.

- Kling 3.0 Pro:

The old man somehow managed to detect a policy violation in one attempt, although the other three generations went through without any problems.

Unfortunately, the result was still the worst of the four.

Kling failed the main instruction every single time: the tongue never actually rotated in a circle.

It moved sideways, twisted, stretched, and performed all kinds of strange anatomical experiments, but it never completed the requested motion.

The image itself looked reasonably realistic, but visual quality was almost irrelevant here. The movement was unnatural, inconsistent, and completely missed the task.

Everything that could go wrong did.

- Grok Imagine 1.5:

This was an unexpectedly good result.

The image still has Grok’s usual slightly cartoonish appearance, but its instruction following was surprisingly strong.

The tongue actually rotated.

Not perfectly, not with completely realistic anatomy, and not always through a clean full circle, but Grok understood what it was supposed to do and made a genuine attempt to execute it.

Considering its performance in several previous tests, this was a very pleasant surprise.

- Gemini Omni Flash:

The only model that handled the task convincingly.

Omni understood the instruction, produced a realistic-looking image, and generated an actual circular tongue movement.

It still isn’t perfect, and the motion does not yet look 100% like something a real person would perform. But compared with the other models, this was easily the cleanest, most controlled, and most believable result.

A genuinely strong performance.

Google finally found a very specific battlefield where Omni Flash can flex.

- Seedance 2.0:

This was the biggest disappointment.

The result was better than Kling’s, but Seedance still failed to perform the requested circular movement.

Seedance remains excellent at large action scenes, complex choreography, and cinematic motion. But in these simple human-body tests, including running and now tongue control, it keeps exposing unexpected weaknesses.

The movement looked more polished than Kling’s, but the core instruction was still not followed.

And for the first time in one of my tests, Seedance finishes below Grok.

- My ranking:

1. Gemini Omni Flash. The best instruction following, the cleanest circular motion, and the most realistic overall result.

2. Grok Imagine 1.5. Not perfect, but it understood the assignment and produced a surprisingly decent attempt.

3. Seedance 2.0. More polished than Kling, but clearly behind Grok and Omni in actual task execution.

4. Kling 3.0 Pro. Censorship, broken anatomy, and almost every possible tongue movement except the one I requested.

What do you think of this test? Do you agree with my ranking?

#AIVideo
